warmup.q: A support worker types "Nrthwind bikes", with a typo, to find the shop Northwind Bikes. The program asks the database for every shop whose name contains "nrthwind", ignoring capitals: WHERE lower(name) LIKE '%nrthwind%', where % stands for any letters. The shops table has an ordinary sorted index on name. What happens?
options: The index finds Northwind Bikes, because the name is in the index
Nothing is found, and the database reads every shop's name to find that out
Northwind Bikes is found and shown first, as the best match
The database refuses the query, because a search must give the first letters of the name
warmup.why: A sorted index keeps whole names in alphabetical order, so it can only jump to names that start with known letters. A % at the front means anything can come first, so the database reads every name. And LIKE matches letters exactly: "nrthwind" isn't inside "northwind", so even reading everything finds nothing, and there's no ranking anyway. Words in any position, typos and best match first need a different index, the one the first section builds.

sections.h: Finding a shop by any word in its name: the inverted index
sections.html:
Let's start with the search box. A small company runs the program that records card payments at shops, and its support team often has to find a shop from whatever a caller says: "the Northwind bike place", or "Nrthwind" with a letter missing. The shops sit in a table called merchants (the code calls a shop a merchant). Its ordinary index on name, the B+tree from the last lesson (a tree of pages that keeps values sorted), keeps whole names in alphabetical order. That's no help here. WHERE lower(name) LIKE '%bike%' asks for names with "bike" anywhere in them (% stands for any letters), and a list sorted by the first letter can't find the middle. The database reads every row, with no idea which match is best.

Version 1 is that scan: read every name and check whether it holds the words. With 2 million shops, every keystroke reads 2 million names, and the results come back in no useful order.

Version 2 turns the data round, the way the index at the back of a book does. The book doesn't list its pages with their words; its index lists the words, each with the pages it's on. Search programs call each thing they search a document, here one shop's name. When a document is added, an analyzer splits its text into tokens, here lower-case words. The index then records, for every token, the documents that contain it and how often. That list is a posting list, and the whole structure is an inverted index: from words to documents, the opposite of a document holding its words.

A query, the text someone searches for, goes through the same analyzer, reads one posting list per word and merges them. The cost follows the length of those lists, not the number of shops. The stepper builds one for five names.

Every index in this lesson is a second copy of the data, arranged for one shape of question and paid for on every write. The shapes are words to documents, time to buckets, a place to what's near it, and a meaning to its nearest neighbours. (The Data models track chose whole stores built around these indexes; here we open the indexes themselves.)

Version 3 ranks the matches. Most search engines use BM25, a scoring formula. For each query word found in a document, it adds idf x tf / (tf + k1 x (1 - b + b x length / average length)). It reads better in words. A rare word counts more than a common one: that's idf, the inverse document frequency. A word that appears twice counts more than once, but not twice as much: tf is the term frequency, and k1 = 1.2 caps it. A match in a short name counts more than one in a long description: b = 0.75 scales by length. Two rules come with it. The analyzer must be the same when indexing and when searching. And typos need fuzzy matching, which accepts words one or two edits away, where an edit adds, removes or changes one letter.

How do new documents get into lists that are kept sorted? The way new keys got into the LSM tree in LSM trees, SSTables and Bloom filters: collect them in memory, write them out as a new file that never changes, and merge files later. Lucene is the free search library inside OpenSearch and Elasticsearch, two popular search programs. It buffers new documents and writes them out as a new segment, a small inverted index of its own that never changes. A search reads every segment and merges the answers. Writing a segment is called a refresh, every second by default in OpenSearch, and that's when a new document becomes searchable. A delete only marks the document in a bitmap, a list of yes-or-no marks, and an update is a delete plus an add. In the background, a merge policy combines segments and drops the deleted documents as it rewrites them, the way an LSM tree's compaction merges its files.

PostgreSQL has an inverted index too, called GIN, as the compare block shows. Words were the first shape of question. Next comes time, where the sorted list works fine and the trouble is that the data never stops arriving.

sections.h: A year of waiting times: cut time into chunks, keep the summaries, drop the rest
sections.html:
Each time a card is tapped, the payments program asks the card's bank for a yes, and it records how long the bank took to answer. That wait is called latency, measured here in milliseconds (ms), thousandths of a second. At 2,000 taps a second, that's 173 million measurements a day. A stream of measurements like this, each stamped with a time, is a time series.

People ask it questions of a fixed shape: the last hour's waits for one shop, a chart in 5-minute steps for the past week, one figure per day for the past year. New points only ever arrive at the current time. Questions ask for a stretch of time, mostly recent. Old points matter only as summaries.

Time is one dimension, so a B+tree can find a stretch of it. That's version 1: one table, with a B+tree index on time. New rows land at the right-hand end of the index, which is fine. The trouble starts with retention, the rule that data is kept for a fixed time and then thrown away. Deleting a day of old rows is 173 million single-row deletes. Each one leaves a dead row version, an old copy no query needs, for VACUUM, PostgreSQL's clean-up job, to remove later (MVCC: versions, snapshots and VACUUM, in the Transactions track, explains why). And the yearly chart reads about 63 billion rows to draw 365 points.

Version 2 splits the table by time, which is called partitioning. TimescaleDB, an add-on for PostgreSQL, turns a table into a hypertable: one table to you, and underneath a separate chunk, a small table of its own, for each stretch of time (one per hour in the Try it). A question about 09:00 to 10:00 opens only the chunk that holds that hour. The planner, the part of PostgreSQL that decides how to run a query, leaves the other 23 out. Retention drops whole chunks, which deletes files instead of rows. That's what add_retention_policy does on a schedule.

Version 3 keeps summaries, which is called downsampling. Cut time into fixed buckets with time_bucket, say 5 minutes each, and keep four numbers per bucket: the count, the sum, the smallest and the largest. Keep sums and counts rather than averages, because sums and counts add up, so twelve 5-minute buckets roll up into an exact hour. Averages don't. Say one bucket had 99 waits averaging 100 ms, and the next had a single wait of 900 ms. The true average is 10,800 / 100 = 108 ms. The average of the two averages is 500 ms, because it weighs one quiet bucket the same as a busy one.

A continuous aggregate keeps those summaries up to date as new rows arrive. It's a materialized view, a stored query result, kept fresh bit by bit (lesson 12 of this track, Materialized views and data cubes, builds them). Then the raw points can expire after a few days, while the hourly summaries stay for years. (The company behind TimescaleDB renamed itself Tiger Data in June 2025, which is why its documentation lives under that name.)

Time runs in one direction, so sorting still works once the table is cut up. A map has two directions, and that breaks the sorted list. Next, we'll see how.

try.title: Watch a hypertable skip chunks, roll up, and forget
steps: From the labs folder, start TimescaleDB: docker compose -f env/timescale.yml up -d --wait. Then load one day of waiting times: docker compose -f env/timescale.yml exec tsdb psql -U sfz -f /sfz/nosql-12-latency.sql (259,200 rows, a few seconds).

Open psql, PostgreSQL's program for typing queries: docker compose -f env/timescale.yml exec tsdb psql -U sfz. Run the statements below one at a time. Predict the number of chunks, how many the 09:00 query opens, and how many hourly rows survive the retention step.
Stop it when you're done: docker compose -f env/timescale.yml down -v.

code.title: in psql
code.html: -- 1. one table to you, 24 chunks underneath: one per hour of data SELECT count(*) AS chunks FROM show_chunks('auth_latency'); -- 2. a question about 09:00 to 10:00 only opens the chunk that holds that hour EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT avg(latency_ms) FROM auth_latency WHERE time >= '2026-11-07 09:00+00' AND time < '2026-11-07 10:00+00'; -- 3. downsample: M-0042's latency in 5-minute buckets, 09:00 to 09:30 SELECT time_bucket('5 minutes', time) AS bucket, count(*) AS n, round(avg(latency_ms)::numeric, 1) AS avg_ms, round(max(latency_ms)::numeric) AS max_ms FROM auth_latency WHERE merchant_id = 'M-0042' AND time >= '2026-11-07 09:00+00' AND time < '2026-11-07 09:30+00' GROUP BY bucket ORDER BY bucket; -- 4. a continuous aggregate: hourly summaries per merchant, kept by TimescaleDB CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW latency_hourly WITH (timescaledb.continuous) AS SELECT time_bucket('1 hour', time) AS bucket, merchant_id, count(*) AS n, sum(latency_ms) AS sum_ms, max(latency_ms) AS max_ms FROM auth_latency GROUP BY bucket, merchant_id; SELECT count(*) AS hourly_rows FROM latency_hourly; -- 5. retention: drop the raw chunks from before 18:00; the hourly summaries stay SELECT count(*) AS chunks_dropped FROM drop_chunks('auth_latency', older_than => TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-07 18:00+00'); SELECT count(*) AS raw_rows FROM auth_latency; SELECT count(*) AS hourly_rows, sum(n) AS points_summarised FROM latency_hourly;

sections.h: Places on a map: one sort order can't hold two directions
sections.html:
A shop in Amsterdam reports a skimmer: someone fitted a fake part to its card reader to copy people's cards. The payments company wants to check every card reader in a box around that shop, about 11 km by 10 km. (The table calls card readers terminals.) Each reader has a latitude, how far north it is, and a longitude, how far east.

Let's try the last lesson's tool first: a B+tree on (lat, lon). It sorts by latitude, and by longitude only among equal latitudes, the column-order rule from Indexes and reading EXPLAIN. So the box's latitude range is one stretch of the index. On the map, that stretch is a band running across the whole width of Europe, and the longitude is checked entry by entry inside it. In the Try it, 1,000,000 card readers spread over Europe put 4,098 entries in the band and 11 in the box. Make the map twice as wide, and the band doubles while the answer stays the same.

Version 2 squeezes two directions into one. A geohash halves the range of longitudes and records which half the point is in, as one bit, a 0 or a 1. Then it does the same for latitude, and so on, taking turns. Every 5 bits become one character from an alphabet of 32. Dam Square, the main square of Amsterdam, is u173z: a cell about 4.9 km tall and 3 km wide, and every point inside it has a geohash that starts with u173z. Points close on the map mostly share a prefix, the first few characters. So an ordinary B+tree on the geohash text answers "near here" with a prefix range, the way a dictionary finds every word that starts with "cat".

Mostly is the catch. Two card readers 10 metres apart, on either side of a cell's edge, can differ from an early character on. The corners of the Try it's box are u173t and u17d0. So a search also has to read the neighbouring cells. The worked example builds a geohash by hand.

Version 3 stops sorting and groups instead. Picture shops filed in envelopes by neighbourhood, inside bigger envelopes by city, each envelope labelled with the area it covers. An R-tree works like that. Each node, a page of the tree, keeps its bounding rectangle, the smallest rectangle around everything below it. A search goes into every child whose rectangle overlaps the box, the way a B+tree goes into the child whose range holds the key. Nearby points share a bottom page, or leaf, whatever their order. PostgreSQL builds R-trees with GiST (generalized search tree), a kit for tree indexes. Each kind of index supplies it a few functions, such as "could this entry match?" and "how do I split a full page?". PostGIS, PostgreSQL's popular add-on for maps, builds its indexes this way.

In the Try it, the GiST index answered the box from 8 pages. It also found "the 5 card readers nearest to Dam Square" from 12 pages, a question a B+tree can't serve at all. Without the GiST index, PostgreSQL measured the distance to all 1,000,000 readers.

Version 4 trades exact shapes for a fixed grid. H3, from the ride-hailing company Uber, covers the globe in hexagons at 16 sizes, called resolutions. Resolution 0 has 122 cells (110 hexagons and 12 pentagons), and each step down splits every cell into 7, so a resolution-9 cell is about 0.1 km². Every card reader gets a cell id, a 64-bit whole number, and "card readers per cell" becomes a GROUP BY, a count per group, on one number column. All six neighbours of a hexagon are the same distance away, which makes heat maps and "everything within two rings" easy. Use H3 for counting and joining by area, and the R-tree for exact boxes and distances.

Two directions break the sorted list. Meaning has hundreds, and next we'll see that even the R-tree gives up there.

try.title: A box and five nearest neighbours: B+tree against GiST
steps: From the labs folder, start PostgreSQL if it isn't running (docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait), and open psql: docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz.

The block creates 1,000,000 card readers with a B+tree on (lat, lon) and a GiST index on a point, PostgreSQL's type for an (x, y) position (about 20 seconds). Before each EXPLAIN, predict the pages read: the box through the B+tree, the box through GiST, and the nearest five with and without GiST.
Drop the table when you're done: DROP TABLE terminals;.

sections.h: Finding by meaning: walk a graph to the nearest neighbours, approximately
sections.html:
A customer writes to support: "charged twice for one bike rental". Support wants past complaints like it, by meaning rather than by shared words. "Duplicate charge, scooter hire" should match, though it shares no word with the first. An inverted index can't do that. An embedding can. A model, a program trained on huge amounts of text, turns each text into a vector: a list of a few hundred to a few thousand numbers, placed so that texts with similar meanings land close together. Each number is one dimension, like north and east on a map, but there are hundreds of them. Photos can be turned into vectors the same way, which is how the photo app found the dogs.

Finding similar complaints becomes finding the nearest vectors to the query, the vector of the new complaint. Close means a small distance, measured one of three ways: Euclidean (L2), the straight-line distance; cosine, the angle between two vectors; or inner product. pgvector, a PostgreSQL add-on that stores and indexes vectors, writes them <->, <=> and <#>. Use the one your embedding model was trained for.

Version 1 is exact: work out the distance from the query to every vector and keep the k smallest, where k is however many you want. The Try it does that over 100,000 vectors of 32 numbers each: 2,138 pages, about 8 ms. With 50 million complaints of 1,536 numbers each, it's 77 billion multiplications and additions for every query.

Version 2 would be an index from the last section, and neither works. A B+tree needs one sort order. An R-tree's rectangles, in hundreds of dimensions, overlap almost any query, so the search opens nearly every node.

Version 3 gives up being exact. Build a graph, a web of links, in which every vector links to some of its nearest neighbours. Search it by walking: start somewhere, move to whichever neighbour is closer to the query, and stop when none is. HNSW (hierarchical navigable small world), from a 2016 paper by Malkov and Yashunin, adds layers, like motorways above town roads. A few vectors sit in the top layer with long links, more in each layer below, and every vector in the bottom one. There the search keeps a beam, a short list of the ef best candidates so far. The stepper walks it.

Three numbers tune HNSW: m, the links per vector (16 in pgvector), ef_construction, the beam while building (64), and hnsw.ef_search, the beam while searching (40). The price is recall, the share of the true nearest neighbours that the search returns. In the Try it, the index read 654 pages in under a millisecond. Its recall@10 (recall among the top 10) was about 0.89 at ef_search = 10, and 1.0 at 40. The index took 41 MB for 17 MB of vectors. Every hop jumps to a random place, so HNSW wants its whole graph in memory.

Filters are the trap. pgvector applies a WHERE clause after the walk: the walk finds ef_search candidates, then the filter drops the ones that don't match. With a filter that keeps about 1 row in 11, LIMIT 10 returned 4 rows on average in the Try it, as pgvector's documentation predicts. Nothing fails and nothing warns you; the answer is quietly short. Since pgvector 0.8.0, SET hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order makes the scan keep walking until enough rows pass, up to hnsw.max_scan_tuples (20,000): 10 of 10.

At a billion vectors, the graph no longer fits in memory. DiskANN (Subramanya and colleagues, 2019) keeps the graph on an SSD, a fast disk with no moving parts, and small compressed copies of the vectors in memory. On one machine with 64 GB of memory, it indexed a billion points and answered over 5,000 queries a second, under 3 ms each on average, at 95% recall@1. The compression is called quantization. The simplest kind stores each number in fewer bits: pgvector's halfvec uses 16 instead of 32, and binary quantization keeps 1. Distances between compressed vectors are rough, so engines re-rank: fetch extra candidates with the small vectors, then sort them by the exact distance.

All four indexes in this lesson find rows, each for its own shape of question, and each costs memory and work on every write. The approximate ones can also miss. None of them decides what happens to the rows once they're found.

try.title: Exact versus HNSW in pgvector, the recall you pay, and a filter
steps: From the labs folder, start PostgreSQL 18 with pgvector 0.8.7: docker compose -f env/pgvector.yml up -d --wait. Then create 100,000 vectors of 32 numbers in 200 clusters (groups of vectors close together), and 20 queries: docker compose -f env/pgvector.yml exec pgv psql -U sfz -f /sfz/nosql-12-vectors.sql (a few seconds).

Open psql with docker compose -f env/pgvector.yml exec pgv psql -U sfz and run the block below. Predict the pages each plan reads, the recall at ef_search 10, 40 and 200, and how many of 10 rows come back when a filter keeps 1 row in 11.
Stop it when you're done: docker compose -f env/pgvector.yml down -v.

code.title: in psql
code.html: -- 1. exact search: compare query 1 with every one of the 100,000 vectors EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF) SELECT id FROM items ORDER BY embedding <-> (SELECT embedding FROM queries WHERE id = 1) LIMIT 10; -- the true top 10 of every query, by brute force (no index exists yet) CREATE TEMP TABLE truth AS SELECT q.id AS qid, i.id FROM queries q CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT id FROM items ORDER BY embedding <-> q.embedding LIMIT 10) i; -- 2. build an HNSW index (pgvector's defaults: m = 16, ef_construction = 64) \timing on CREATE INDEX items_hnsw ON items USING hnsw (embedding vector_l2_ops); \timing off -- 3. the same query, through the index EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF) SELECT id FROM items ORDER BY embedding <-> (SELECT embedding FROM queries WHERE id = 1) LIMIT 10; -- 4. recall@10: what share of the true top 10 does the index find, at three beam widths? CREATE TEMP VIEW recall AS SELECT current_setting('hnsw.ef_search') AS ef_search, round(avg(found) / 10.0, 3) AS recall_at_10 FROM (SELECT q.id, count(t.id) AS found FROM queries q CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT id FROM items ORDER BY embedding <-> q.embedding LIMIT 10) a LEFT JOIN truth t ON t.qid = q.id AND t.id = a.id GROUP BY q.id) r; SET hnsw.ef_search = 10; SELECT * FROM recall; SET hnsw.ef_search = 40; SELECT * FROM recall; SET hnsw.ef_search = 200; SELECT * FROM recall; -- 5. a filter that keeps about 1 item in 11, in every cluster: how many of 10 rows come back? SET hnsw.ef_search = 40; CREATE TEMP VIEW filtered AS SELECT current_setting('hnsw.iterative_scan') AS iterative_scan, round(avg(n), 1) AS avg_rows_back FROM queries q CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT count(*) AS n FROM (SELECT id FROM items WHERE id % 11 = 0 ORDER BY embedding <-> q.embedding LIMIT 10) a) c; SELECT * FROM filtered; SET hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order; SELECT * FROM filtered;

 40        |        1.000

 ef_search | recall_at_10
-----------+--------------
 200       |        1.000

 iterative_scan | avg_rows_back
----------------+---------------
 off            |           4.0

 iterative_scan | avg_rows_back
----------------+---------------
 relaxed_order  |          10.0

The exact query read all 100,000 vectors (2,138 pages, in two processes at once) and sorted them by distance to keep 10. Through the HNSW index it read 654 pages and ran about ten times faster. The index found every true neighbour at ef_search 40 and 200, and about 89% of them at 10. That number moves from build to build, because HNSW picks layers at random (0.955 on another run). With the filter, the walk collected 40 candidates and the filter kept about 4, so LIMIT 10 came back short. The iterative scan kept walking and returned all 10. Times depend on your machine; the page counts, the recall at 40 and the 4.0 are what to look at.

video.title: Nearest by meaning: walking a graph from the top layer down

opening:
Picture an afternoon with your phone. You type "nrthwind bikes" into a map app, typo and all, and it finds Northwind Bikes. It shows the five bike shops nearest to where you're standing. A fitness app draws a chart of your last year of runs in a blink. Your photo app finds every picture with a dog in it, though you never labelled one.

Each answer comes back from millions of records in under a second. It's tempting to think the app uses the same index as always, a sorted list, only bigger. A sorted list can't do any of these. It finds a name that starts with "North". It can't find one with a typo, a shop near you, or a photo like another.

In Indexes and reading EXPLAIN, we built that sorted list and met its limit: it only answers questions about its one order. In this lesson, we'll build a different index for each of four kinds of question: words, time, places and meaning. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a phone that found a shop through a typo, the nearest bike shops, a year of runs and a dog in a photo. Each answer came from its own index: posting lists for words, chunks and summaries for time, rectangles or hexagons for places, and a walk through a graph for meaning.

Next time a search box forgives your typo, try a word from the middle of a name, then the same word with one letter changed. If both still find it, there's an inverted index with fuzzy matching behind the box.

Next, we'll follow the rows after an index finds them. Why can a query with LIMIT 5 stop after reading 62 rows of 100,000?

compare.title: "northwind bikes" in PostgreSQL full-text search and in OpenSearch

a.label: PostgreSQL 18: GIN index
a.title: psql
a.html: -- a GIN index is an inverted index: one entry per lexeme, pointing at the rows CREATE INDEX merchants_name_fts ON merchants USING gin (to_tsvector('english', name)); SELECT id, round(ts_rank(to_tsvector('english', name), q)::numeric, 4) AS rank FROM merchants, plainto_tsquery('english', 'northwind bikes') AS q WHERE to_tsvector('english', name) @@ q ORDER BY rank DESC; -- id | rank -- --------+-------- -- M-0042 | 0.1878

b.label: OpenSearch 3.9: match query
b.title: curl
b.html: curl -s 'localhost:9200/merchants/_search?filter_path=hits.hits._id,hits.hits._score' \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{ "query": { "match": { "name": "northwind bikes" } } }' # {"hits":{"hits":[{"_id":"M-0042","_score":0.62533486}, # {"_id":"M-0043","_score":0.5064695},{"_id":"M-0045","_score":0.4883092}]}}

compare.note: Both are inverted indexes over the same five names, and both answers are real output (PostgreSQL 18 in a throwaway container, OpenSearch from the Try it). PostgreSQL's GIN index holds one entry per lexeme, its word for a word cut back to its stem. plainto_tsquery requires every word, so PostgreSQL returns only M-0042. Ask for either word with websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'northwind or bikes') and it returns four rows, M-0044 included, because its english stemmer turns "Bike" and "Bikes" into the same lexeme. ts_rank isn't BM25: it ignores how rare a word is across the table. OpenSearch's match query asks for any of the words, ranked by BM25, with fuzzy matching and an analyzer per field to hand. For a shop directory inside one PostgreSQL database, the first is often enough. For typo-tolerant, ranked search over millions of documents, use the second.

worked.title: Compute a geohash by hand, then in Kotlin

steps.say: Start with Dam Square, latitude 52.373 and longitude 4.893. Each step halves a range and records which half the point is in: 1 for the upper half, 0 for the lower. Longitude goes first, then the two take turns.
steps.code:
bit 1  lon 4.893  in [-180, 180]  mid 0       -> 1, keep [0, 180]
bit 2  lat 52.373 in [-90, 90]    mid 0       -> 1, keep [0, 90]
bit 3  lon        in [0, 180]     mid 90      -> 0, keep [0, 90]
bit 4  lat        in [0, 90]      mid 45      -> 1, keep [45, 90]
bit 5  lon        in [0, 90]      mid 45      -> 0, keep [0, 45]

steps.say: Five bits make one character. The alphabet is the digits and the letters without a, i, l and o, so 11010, which is 26, is u. The next five bits, 00001, are 1: the cell u1 covers latitudes 50.6 to 56.3 and longitudes 0 to 11.25.
Keep going to 25 bits and the geohash is u173z, a cell 0.044 degrees on each side: 4.9 km north to south and, this far north, 3.0 km east to west. Six characters would be about 610 m by 750 m.
The same steps in Kotlin. Each turn of the loop produces one bit, and every fifth bit closes a character.
steps.code: fun geohash(lat: Double, lon: Double, chars: Int): String { val base32 = "0123456789bcdefghjkmnpqrstuvwxyz" val latRange = doubleArrayOf(-90.0, 90.0) val lonRange = doubleArrayOf(-180.0, 180.0) val out = StringBuilder() var bits = 0 var nBits = 0 var lonTurn = true // longitude first, then alternate while (out.length < chars) { val range = if (lonTurn) lonRange else latRange val v = if (lonTurn) lon else lat val mid = (range[0] + range[1]) / 2 bits = bits shl 1 if (v >= mid) { bits = bits or 1; range[0] = mid } else range[1] = mid lonTurn = !lonTurn if (++nBits == 5) { out.append(base32[bits]); bits = 0; nBits = 0 } // 5 bits: one character } return out.toString() } geohash(52.373, 4.893, 5) // "u173z"

steps.say: Use it with a B+tree. Store the geohash in a column, index it, and ask for the cell as a prefix range. Then deal with the edges: the Try it's box has corners u173t and u17d0, so one prefix is never enough. Search the cell and its eight neighbours, and check the exact distance on the rows that come back.
steps.code: -- every terminal in cell u173z, through an ordinary B+tree on geohash SELECT id FROM terminals WHERE geohash >= 'u173z' AND geohash < 'u1740'; -- near a cell edge: query u173z and its 8 neighbours, then filter by real distance

lab.title: Build an inverted index with BM25, a downsampler, and an approximate vector search
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. No Docker needed. Three tests pass, because they test code you're given (tokenize, bucketStart, retain), and fourteen fail.

In InvertedIndex.kt, write add (tokens, length, one posting per distinct term) and search (BM25, as the KDoc comment describes it). The search test checks your scores against the ones OpenSearch returned in the Try it. All six tests in InvertedIndexTest pass.
In TimeSeries.kt, write downsample and rollup. The rollup test gives a busy bucket and a quiet one, and checks that you didn't average the averages. All six in TimeSeriesTest pass.

In VectorSearch.kt, write ExactSearch.search, then GraphIndex.search: the beam search from the stepper's last two frames. The tests build a graph over 2,000 clustered vectors and check recall@10 at different beam sizes. All seventeen pass.
Experiment: in the beam search, stop as soon as the closest candidate is farther than the BEST result instead of the worst. Watch recall fall, then put it back.
hints: add: tokens.groupingBy { it }.eachCount() gives the term frequencies, and postings.getOrPut(term) { mutableListOf() } += Posting(docId, tf) files each one.
search: keep a HashMap<String, Double> of scores and merge(docId, part, Double::plus). Sort with compareByDescending<Hit> { it.score }.thenBy { it.docId }.
downsample: points.groupBy { bucketStart(it.at, width) }, then build a Bucket from each group's values. rollup is the same with it.start, adding up counts and sums.

Beam search: two PriorityQueues with the file's closestFirst comparator, one as it is (candidates) and one with closestFirst.reversed() (the best so far, worst on top). visited.add(id) returns false if you've seen it.
Every distance(...) you compute must also do distanceCalls++: the tests check that the graph search computes far fewer distances than the exact one.
lab.done: All seventeen tests in InvertedIndexTest, TimeSeriesTest and VectorSearchTest pass.

drill.title: BM25 and a rollup by hand
drill.prompt: Without looking: (a) write BM25's score for one query term in one document, and say in a phrase what idf, k1 and b each do. (b) Two documents contain "northwind" once each; one is 2 tokens long and the other 7, and the average is 4.2. Which ranks first, and why? (c) Two 5-minute buckets have (count 99, sum 9,900) and (count 1, sum 900). What's the hourly average, and what would averaging the averages give?

answer.html:
(a) idf(t) * tf / (tf + k1 * (1 - b + b * len / avglen))
    idf = ln(1 + (N - n + 0.5) / (n + 0.5)): rare terms count more
    k1 (1.2): saturates repeats, so the 10th occurrence adds little
    b (0.75): how much a long document is penalised for its length
(b) the 2-token one: same tf and idf, smaller length -> smaller denominator
    (0.506 against 0.313 in the lesson's five merchants)
(c) (9,900 + 900) / (99 + 1) = 108
    averaging the averages: (100 + 900) / 2 = 500, wrong, because it weights
    one quiet bucket like 99 busy ones. Keep count and sum, never the average.

recap: A B+tree answers questions about one sort order. Every index in this lesson is another copy of the data, arranged for a different shape of question and paid for on every write.

An inverted index maps each word to a posting list of the documents that contain it, and BM25 ranks matches by rarity, repeats and length. Lucene writes it as segments that never change: a refresh makes new ones searchable, and merges combine them, like an LSM tree's compaction.
Time-series stores split a table into chunks by time, keep the count, sum, smallest and largest per bucket, roll buckets up into bigger ones, and drop whole old chunks. Never average averages.

A B+tree on (lat, lon) walks a whole band of latitudes. Geohashes turn a map cell into a text prefix, R-trees (GiST in PostgreSQL) group nearby points under rectangles and find nearest neighbours, and H3 gives every place a whole-number cell id.

HNSW walks a layered graph with a beam (in pgvector: m 16, ef_construction 64, ef_search 40). It trades recall for speed, wants its graph in memory, and filters after the walk, so a narrow filter returns too few rows unless iterative scans are on.

The limit: at a billion vectors the graph leaves memory (DiskANN keeps it on SSD, with compressed vectors in memory and a re-rank), every approximate index can miss, and no index decides what to do with the rows it finds.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks why we can't use ordinary B+tree indexes for shop search, the skimming map and "similar complaints". Explain what each of those three questions needs from an index, and what each special index gives up.
explain.answer: A B+tree keeps one sort order, so it only helps with equality, ranges and prefixes in that order. Shop search needs words in any position, typos and ranking. An inverted index keeps a posting list per word, so a query reads a few lists instead of every name, and BM25 ranks by rarity and length. It's written in segments that never change, so new shops show up after a refresh, and deleted ones take space until a merge. The skimming map needs two directions at once. A B+tree on latitude and longitude walks a whole band of latitudes across the map, while an R-tree (GiST in PostgreSQL) groups nearby card readers under rectangles, reads only the ones that overlap, and can also find the nearest readers. Similar complaints need nearest neighbours among embeddings with hundreds of dimensions, where neither a sort order nor rectangles help. HNSW walks a graph and gives up a little recall for a large speed-up, needs its graph in memory, and applies filters after the walk, so a filtered query can come back short unless iterative scans are on. Each one is an extra structure that every write must update, so I'd start inside PostgreSQL (full-text search, GiST, pgvector) and measure.

deeper.html:
Posting lists are squeezed hard, because most of a search index is posting lists. Lucene stores document ids as gaps from the previous id, packs those small numbers into blocks of bits, and keeps skip data, so that combining a rare word's list with a common one can jump ahead instead of reading every entry. A query for two words is closer to a merge with skips than to a scan.

Lucene 10.3's default merge policy, TieredMergePolicy, merges segments of about the same size, up to 10 at a time, and aims for about 8 segments of each size. Without merging, a busy index would pile up thousands of small segments, and every search would read them all.

Percentiles don't roll up the way sums do. The 99th percentile is the value that 99% of waits stay under, and you can't combine two buckets' 99th percentiles into the hour's. Time-series systems keep a small sketch per bucket instead, a summary that can be merged, such as a t-digest or a histogram with fixed edges. If a promise to customers is written as a percentile ("99% of answers within 300 ms"), check that your store keeps sketches rather than stored percentiles. InfluxDB 3 does the job of TimescaleDB on Apache Arrow and Parquet files, which store data by column, and the Cassandra tables split by day in the Data models track are the same idea done by hand.

Space-filling curves are the general idea behind geohashes. The Z-shaped path that alternating bits trace jumps at every cell edge. A Hilbert curve visits cells in an order where each cell touches the next, so a box maps to fewer, longer ranges of the one-dimensional key. Bkd-trees, which Lucene uses for numbers and map points, split space by alternating directions, like a k-d tree, and store the leaves in blocks on disk. GiST's kit has five functions an index type must supply, among them consistent (could this entry match the query?), union (the rectangle around these entries) and picksplit (how to split a full node).

HNSW isn't the only approximate index. IVF (inverted file) indexes group the vectors around centroids, points that stand for each group, and a search compares the query with the centroids and scans only the nearest few groups (ivfflat.lists, a good start being rows / 1000, and ivfflat.probes, default 1, in pgvector). They build faster and use less memory than HNSW, and usually need more tuning for the same recall. Product quantization (Jégou and colleagues, 2011) cuts a vector into pieces and replaces each piece by the id of its nearest centroid, so 128 numbers become 8 bytes. Graph indexes can also fail on strongly clustered data. While this lesson's Try it was being written, vectors in 200 tight, well-separated clusters left recall stuck at 0.90 even at ef_search = 200, because two queries never reached their cluster from the entry point. More links per vector (m) is the usual remedy.

Every index in this lesson can also live outside your main database, in a search cluster or a vector database. Then it's a copy that falls behind, and it has to be fed from the system of record without writing twice; the Derived data track builds that properly.
